sentences.text: Dromaeosaurus was a sturdy, wolf-sized predator with a short, solid skull that resembled a miniature Tyrannosaurus.
This carnivore measured between 1.80 and 2 meters in length and weighed approximately 15 to 16 kilograms.
It possessed an intermediate-sized sickle claw for gripping prey and was almost certainly covered in feathers.
Despite appearing frequently in museum displays and media, the animal is actually known from surprisingly few real fossils.
Its name comes from the Greek words dromeus, meaning runner, and sauros, meaning lizard.
The first remains were found by Barnum Brown in 1914 near the Red Deer River in Alberta, leading to the description of the type species Dromaeosaurus albertensis in 1922.
Matthew and Brown originally placed this dinosaur in the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae within the family Deinodontidae.
Research by Therrien, Ruff, and Henderson in 2005 estimated that Dromaeosaurus had a bite force nearly three times stronger than that of Velociraptor.
Studies of tooth wear suggest it used a puncture and pull method to eat bone, unlike troodontids that preferred softer food.
The animal had notably large eyes for good vision, well-developed smell and hearing, and a rigid tail that allowed it to run at speeds over 40 km/h.
Its tail was stiff except at the base, using thin bone rods to act as a rudder for quick turns and jumps.
Dromaeosaurus could hunt prey similar to or larger than itself, such as ornithomimids and juvenile ceratopsians, while also eating smaller animals like lizards.
The discovery of the sister species Dakotaraptor supports the idea that Dromaeosaurus relied less on its sickle claw than other dromaeosaurids.
In 1969, John H. Ostrom assigned Dromaeosaurus to the family Dromaeosauridae based on shared features with Velociraptor and Deinonychus.
Dromaeosaurus albertensis is the type specimen and the most complete known member, and the family name is derived from it.
Teeth attributed to this species have been found in the Prince Creek Formation, where it lived in what is now North America.
Dromaeosaurus lived from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 110.1 and 66 million years ago.

It is debated whether unusual, grooved teeth found in Alberta belong to Dromaeosaurus, and scientists argue whether its robust construction makes it appear primitive despite being a highly specialized animal.
